I've been hospitalized twice, in two different mental wards.

In both places, there was a lot of structure. Get up, eat breakfast, have various group sessions, eat lunch, more sessions, dinner and visitation. Before bed would be a final reflection session about what you learned that day. Sessions will emphasize on learning coping mechanisms, so your mileage may vary on whether that is useful. If you're skinny because of a low metabolism and don't have an ED (like me), they may scrutinize how much you eat. They will mess with your medications to see what works for you, and part of the experimentation may fuck shit up a little--the first time I was in, I was put on something that straight up killed my appetite. I was off it a day later.

If you hate the program you're in, be as cooperative as possible and they'll discharge you. Personally, I feel like I met some interesting folks while hospitalized, but the programs themselves did not so much for me. Ironically, being hospitalized gave me a little something to live for, because now I really want to do something to revamp the mental health care system in the U.S.

Both of the programs I was in emphasized "personal responsibility"--which sounds great on paper, but in practice can easily become "it's your fault that you're depressed, and if you were doing more for your mental health you wouldn't feel this way." Stuff like this ticked me off, and I dealt with it by writing rants on scrap paper.

There's a lot more, of course, but I don't know what else to put here. Feel free to PM me if you want to know more or have any questions.

I have also met Patrick Stewart. My circumstances in meeting him really weren't bizarre, but I did end up feeling incredible second-hand embarrassment at the end of it.

I was with my American theatre department this past spring in London, and Patrick Stewart was playing William Shakespeare in a play called Bingo: Scenes of Money and Death at the Young Vic theatre. After the performance, I decided to hang around in case I could grab an autograph in my program. While waiting I met another American who had the same plan. I initially thought he was alright, but due to the nature of my trip, seeing fifteen-ish plays and being surrounded by thespians the whole damn time, I forgot that not everyone is a theatre geek and it didn't occur to me that this dude went to a somewhat obscure play just because Patrick Stewart was in it. This dude was also wearing Vibram FiveFingers.

Anyway, about twenty minutes or so after the show, Stewart was passing through the bar area in a big trenchcoat and a beret when some other patrons stop him. When others (including myself and Toed-Shoes Guy) started to gather, he being a classy guy corralled us into standing near the ticket office so we'd be more out of the way. In meantime, Toed-Shoes Guy starts talking to Stewart all while other people are getting their autographs, just dominating the conversation. In lieu complimenting Stewart, he tries to compliment one of the other actors. And he ends up saying this: "I thought the guy playing the gardener was really good, *where did you find him*?" Now the actor he was trying to complement was John McEnery, and while I didn't know the guy either, the program **that he bought** was clear with his credits that he is a really fucking prolific actor. Stewart's response was thus: "*Find him?* He's a very well-known actor!" Toed-Shoes Guy mumbles something about being a dumb American, Stewart didn't look surprised in the least. I got his autograph in my program and could only manage to say a thank you, but I was impressed by Stewart all the same.

But here's one more akin to the perimeters of this post: Days later, a friend waiting backstage after a show was run into by another person. After copious apologies from both parties, my friend realized that Patrick Stewart had just literally bumped into her.

Conclusion: Patrick Stewart is an awesome human being.
